question: Can one-phase online SGD learn an extensive collection of orthogonal Gaussian single-index tasks with unequal strengths in polynomial time, and can the superposition of their sharp recovery events produce explicit training-time, sample, width, and compute scaling laws?

key_findings.claim: Under strong dimensional, width, initialization, accuracy, and learning-rate conditions, online SGD assigns selected student neurons to teacher directions by a greedy weighted-overlap rule, keeps unused neurons small, and recovers each selected direction and coefficient in a narrow relative time window.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2.1 places the transition for selected pair p at T_p equal to the inverse of 4 I(I-1) times the squared leading Hermite coefficient, signal strength, learning rate, and initial squared overlap raised to I-1. Before (1-Delta/256)T_p, direction and norm remain small; after (1+Delta/4)T_p, squared overlap is at least 1-epsilon_D and squared norm is within epsilon_R of the matched teacher coefficient. Appendix D proves these statements by stochastic induction, martingale concentration, and separate control of relevant, irrelevant, and unused coordinates.

key_findings.claim: The informal headline reverses the dependence of sample and runtime complexity on signal strength, and the printed learning-rate summary drops required inverse polynomial suppression.
key_findings.evidence: Page 3 twice prints n and T proportional to a squared, including a_min squared for all tasks, which would make weaker signals faster; Theorem 2.1's event times and the page-7 summary instead scale inversely with signal, so both headline occurrences require a^{-2}. Page 7 also prints eta as a_min d^{-I} times poly(m,P), while the theorem's bound and runtime require division by polynomial width and problem factors. These are substantive direction-of-scaling errors, not hidden-constant choices.

key_findings.claim: The single-phase MSE dynamics behave like automatic deflation: once one teacher component is fitted, its residual signal is removed, which approximately decouples later tasks despite extensive width and a diverging coefficient condition number.
key_findings.evidence: The student uses a 2-homogeneous parameterization whose first-layer norm squared is also its output coefficient. The population gradient decomposes into radial and tangent parts. Row, column, and threshold gaps in the greedy maximum-selection matrix ensure each intended overlap escapes first; after its norm fits the coefficient, the residual from that teacher direction becomes negligible and competing coordinates stop growing. Appendices C and D maintain the required blockwise bounds for gradient flow and online SGD.

key_findings.claim: The main theorem measures minimum strength over the teacher prefix while its dynamics learn a greedy selected set, leaving the stated terminal-time bound unsupported without an added selection theorem or a changed minimum.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2.1 defines a_min* over indices 1 through P* but fits coefficients a_{pi(p)} for a greedily selected mapping pi. The page-84 T_max bound needs every selected a_{pi(p)} to exceed that prefix minimum, which the theorem's general coefficient assumptions do not establish; Appendix E later proves only a weaker top-signal fact for the special power law. Induction Hypothesis D.1(b) compounds the mismatch by writing a_p where the theorem and dynamics require a_{pi(p)}.

key_findings.claim: The initialization-gap lemma that supports the claimed event ordering is not proved by the displayed probability arguments.
key_findings.evidence: The row-gap proof ends with exponent 2 instead of the score exponent 2I-2. The column-gap displays replace the required denominator z_{l,p} with z_{k,l}. The threshold-gap proof likewise substitutes z_{k,l}, misindexes the second teacher overlap, and concludes with the unweighted column-gap event. The regularity argument also treats greedily coupled row-use events as independent without justification. Because these gaps feed the continuous and stochastic inductions, the paper's event-order guarantee must be treated as author-claimed rather than independently established by the printed proof.

anchors.section: B, Lemma 3.1 row and column gaps

key_findings.claim: For square-summable power-law teacher strengths a_p proportional to p^{-beta} with beta greater than one half, individual directions emerge at progressively later times and their aggregate population loss follows a power law until the finite-width approximation floor.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 2.2 states that direction p among the learnable top order-m directions is recovered at time tilde-Theta(p^beta d^{I-1}/eta). Across the interval in which most directions are learned, loss is bounded above and below by constants times the sum of an order-(m/log m)^{1-2 beta} width term and an order-(eta t/d^{I-1})^{(1-2 beta)/beta} optimization term, up to epsilon_D. Appendix E proves that sufficiently strong teacher directions enter the greedy selection and integrates the remaining p^{-2 beta} tail.

key_findings.claim: When the learning rate is chosen for a prespecified sample budget and only the strongest recoverable directions, the paper derives a faster but horizon-dependent sample scaling whose beta exponent matches Gaussian-sequence and linear-SGD analyses.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary 2.3 chooses eta as a function of n and m and gives loss of tilde-Theta of m^{1-2 beta} plus (n divided by d^{2I-1} times a polynomial in P)^{(1-2 beta)/(2 beta)}, up to epsilon_D. The paper calls the choice unstable because it is intentionally too large for weaker directions outside the selected prefix and does not provide an anytime decaying schedule.

key_findings.claim: The finite-dimensional population-gradient simulation is qualitatively consistent with the predicted compute-optimal slope, but it is a single synthetic setting rather than an online-SGD sample-complexity experiment.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 compares an idealized staircase construction with population-loss gradient descent at d=2048, P=1024, Hermite-4 activation, beta=0.8, and several student widths. The displayed empirical frontier has slope about -0.36 versus the theoretical -0.33. The paper reports no repetitions, error bars, scalar fit protocol, fresh-sample SGD run, or held-out generalization evaluation.

key_findings.claim: The exact v2 artifact contains normalization, constant-factor, and general-information-exponent inconsistencies; its beta exponents are plausible intended scalings, not a fully verified consequence of the printed proof.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 requires sum_p a_p^2=1. Proposition 2.2 defines a_p=p^{-beta}/Z with Z=sum p^{-2beta}, omitting the square root, while Appendix E gives incompatible Z=sum p^beta. The MSE has a factor one half and page 88 derives half-scaled loss bounds, but Theorem 2.1 states one minus the full learned mass. Appendix E also omits the 2I-2 event-time exponent on page 94, uses a union where an all-row intersection is required on page 95, changes an overlap exponent on page 96, and replaces d^{I-1} by d on page 97. These defects leave the intended tail heuristic recognizable but do not verify the displayed general-I derivation.

key_findings.claim: The gradient-flow event-time restatement contains the opposite dimension dependence from its own exact definition.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem C.1 first defines T_p as inverse in a_{pi(p)} times the initial overlap to power 2I-2. Since squared random overlap is order 1/d, this is order d^{I-1}/a. Pages 30 and 32 instead print order 1/(a d^{I-1}). Induction Hypothesis C.2(c) on page 30 additionally bounds a selected norm using undefined index l.

anchors.section: C, Theorem C.1 and Induction Hypothesis C.2

key_findings.claim: A second sign error appears only in the prose interpretation of the compute frontier: the displayed equation and plot show decreasing loss, while the following sentence prints a positive one-third exponent.
key_findings.evidence: Page 8 derives L proportional to total compute raised to (1-2 beta)/(1+beta), which equals -1/3 at beta=0.8. Figure 2 labels the theoretical slope -0.33 and empirical slope -0.36. The page-9 sentence nevertheless writes L proportional to (mt)^{1/3}; the consistent value is (mt)^{-1/3}.

method.core_idea: Turn many hard single-index searches into a controlled event-time process: use a 2-homogeneous student whose coefficient grows only after directional alignment, prove that random-initialization gaps select one student-teacher pair at a time, and integrate the coefficient mass of the tasks whose emergence times have passed.
method.mechanism: For an even activation whose first nonzero Hermite term has degree 2I greater than two, early overlap x approximately follows dx/dt proportional to a x^I, so a random overlap of order 1/d stays near initialization and then escapes sharply at time proportional to d^{I-1}/a. A greedy maximum over coefficient-weighted initial overlaps predicts the event order. Population-gradient calculations split each update into radial and tangent components; continuous induction controls the three off-diagonal blocks, and stochastic induction plus martingale bounds couples online SGD to the gradient-flow escape times. Once a selected direction aligns, its norm squared rapidly fits the teacher coefficient, removing that residual component. Power-law coefficients then map rank p to event time p^beta and make the unlearned squared-coefficient tail a training-loss power law.
assumptions: Inputs are fresh independent samples from the isotropic Gaussian N(0,I_d), and the objective is population or online-sample squared error.
Teacher directions are exactly orthonormal and teacher coefficients are nonnegative and ordered.
The activation is even, sufficiently smooth, polynomially bounded, normalized in Gaussian L2, and has information exponent 2I greater than two with a nonvanishing leading Hermite coefficient.
The student is a specially coupled 2-homogeneous two-layer network with positive coefficient ||v_k||^2, tiny spherical initialization d^{-C}, and no independent output weights.
Dimension, teacher and student widths, coefficient minimum, target errors, and failure probability obey the detailed polynomial separation conditions in Theorem 2.1.
The online-SGD learning rate is much smaller than a_min times d^{-I} and also carries inverse polynomial factors in m, P, failure probability, and overlap gaps.
The stable power-law statement assumes beta greater than one half; the heavy-tailed beta below one half discussion requires student width roughly proportional to teacher width.
The compute-optimal statement treats one gradient step as cost proportional to student width and suppresses dimension and other polynomial factors.

techniques.role: Rewrites Gaussian population MSE and its gradients as sums over even Hermite degrees, exposing the leading information-exponent dynamics.
Couples output-coefficient growth to directional alignment so norms remain tiny during search and later fit teacher strengths automatically.
Orders student-teacher pairs by coefficient times initial overlap power to predict which direction escapes next.
Uses row, column, and threshold gaps to keep upper-triangular, lower-triangular, and unused-task overlaps below their intended competitors.
Maintains incoherence, norm, and relevance invariants throughout the population gradient-flow trajectory.
Controls sample-gradient noise with stopped processes and interval-wise variance bounds so online SGD preserves sharp event ordering.
Makes a fitted teacher component cease driving other neurons without an explicit stage change or reinitialization.
Converts power-law-ranked teacher strengths into aggregate optimization, width, sample, and compute exponents.

evaluations.setting: Idealized decoupled emergence model with beta=0.8 and multiple student widths.
evaluations.metric: Population loss against total compute, with the compute-optimal envelope on log-log axes.
evaluations.result: The staircase sum approaches a smooth tail and the displayed optimal envelope has slope about -0.33 before reaching width-dependent floors.
evaluations.baseline: The closed-form event-time and truncated power-law-tail prediction from Section 3.1.

evaluations.setting: Finite-dimensional population-loss gradient descent with d=2048, P=1024, Hermite-4 activation, beta=0.8, and varied student width.
evaluations.metric: Population MSE versus width times gradient-descent steps and slope of the compute-optimal envelope.
evaluations.result: The plotted empirical envelope has slope about -0.36, qualitatively near the predicted -0.33, and individual width curves show plateaus after their descending region.
evaluations.baseline: The idealized decoupled scaling curves and theoretical compute-optimal slope.

limitations: Author-stated: the analysis requires isotropic Gaussian inputs; anisotropic covariance and a second spectral power law are left open.
Author-stated: the high-information-exponent requirement excludes information exponent two, where task decoupling changes; a separate quadratic-activation companion handles that special case.
Author-stated: the budget-dependent unstable discretization is not an anytime algorithm, and a decaying schedule that achieves it at every horizon remains open.

Reviewer inference: exact orthogonality, even smooth activations, nonnegative coefficients, fresh online samples, and the coupled 2-homogeneous parameterization exclude common shallow-network and modern deep-learning settings.
Reviewer inference: the theorem's learning rate is suppressed by several inverse width and failure-probability factors; the headline polynomial guarantee does not imply a practically usable rate.
Reviewer inference: Figure 2 uses population gradient descent rather than the online SGD process covered by the main theorem and reports one synthetic configuration without repetitions or error bars.
Reviewer inference: the paper establishes optimization and population loss in a realizable noiseless teacher model, not finite-dataset generalization, robustness, misspecification, or transfer.

Contradiction audit: the informal sample/runtime formulas reverse the signal-strength dependence, the learning-rate prose drops inverse polynomial suppression, and the selected-set minimum in Theorem 2.1 is not justified by its general assumptions.

Contradiction audit: the row, column, threshold, and regularity gap arguments on pages 25-27 contain exponent, denominator, index, event, and independence defects that feed the later event-order inductions.

Contradiction audit: the v2 PDF has incompatible power-law normalizers, a factor-two loss mismatch, reversed dimension scaling in Theorem C.1, several Appendix E event/exponent defects, and a missing minus sign in the page-9 compute-scaling sentence.

Reviewer inference: the exact pinned source is the 97-page arXiv v2 artifact; the official NeurIPS 2025 version of record is a distinct 83-page proceedings artifact and must not be silently substituted for it.
failure_modes: If teacher directions are correlated rather than orthogonal, several neurons can be attracted to mixtures or a shared average and the greedy blockwise decoupling can fail.
If the activation has information exponent two, second-order rotational structure can learn a subspace jointly rather than isolate one direction per sharp event.
Odd activations reintroduce hemisphere/sign issues that the even-link assumption removes.
Independent or signed output weights can grow before directional recovery and invalidate the automatic-deflation timing used by the proof.
A larger practical learning rate can let martingale fluctuations erase the small initialization gaps and reorder or merge emergence events.
The greedy selected set can include a coefficient below the theorem's prefix-based a_min*, invalidating the stated common terminal-time bound.
Malformed or unjustified initialization-gap events can break the induction before any stochastic-gradient coupling argument applies.
Without a broad power-law range in coefficient strengths, the aggregate loss is a finite staircase or crossover rather than a stable macroscopic power law.
Finite reused datasets add sample covariance and overfitting effects absent from the fresh-sample population analysis.
Using the printed normalizers literally violates the coefficient normalization and changes exact loss constants, while using the printed positive compute exponent contradicts the plotted decay.
Applying the Appendix E displays beyond information exponent I=2 inherits omitted overlap powers and a final d-versus-d^{I-1} substitution.
reusable_insights: Model a smooth aggregate scaling curve as the survival tail of many discrete learning events, then test event times and event masses separately.
A coupled homogeneous parameterization can turn simultaneous optimization into implicit deflation without explicit stage boundaries.
When stochastic dynamics must preserve an event ordering, controlling noise only up to a constant-factor hitting time is insufficient; the concentration scale must resolve the smallest ordering gap.
Separate approximation floors from optimization tails before fitting a single scaling exponent.
For budget-aware learning-rate choices, state explicitly whether the result is anytime or horizon-specific.
Audit exact constants and normalization independently from asymptotic exponents; a plausible exponent can coexist with an incomplete displayed proof.
open_questions: Can the emergence-time theory survive anisotropic or non-Gaussian inputs when task directions and covariance eigenvectors are not aligned?
Can one prove comparable sequential deflation for conventional networks with independent signed output weights?
Is there an anytime learning-rate schedule that attains the unstable sample exponent without knowing the final budget?
How do correlated teacher directions change the event order, and when do they create mixture attractors rather than distinct recovered features?
Can the online population result be extended to a fixed reused dataset with explicit generalization and interpolation phases?
Do realistic networks exhibit coefficient-weighted initialization gaps and per-feature residual removal that predict measured emergence times?
Can the exact normalization and factor-two defects be corrected in a future source revision without changing the stated asymptotic theorems?
Can the authors repair the initialization-gap proof and selected-set minimum without changing the greedy event order or sample-complexity statement?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning sum of diverse features: computational hardness and efficient gradient-based training for ridge combinations
competitive_landscape.difference: Oko et al. prove polynomial learnability and SQ hardness for extensive sums of diverse near-orthogonal ridge functions, but their efficient method is layer-wise and can require severe overparameterization as component strengths become ill-conditioned. The reviewed paper narrows to one shared even link and exactly orthogonal directions but trains both layers in one MSE phase and derives sharp per-direction event times and scaling laws.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Orthogonal Multi-Index Models: A Fine-Grained Information Exponent Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Ren and Lee show that second- and higher-order Hermite terms can first recover the relevant subspace and then exact directions in a narrow orthogonal multi-index regime, improving a naive information-exponent rate. The reviewed paper studies extensive width, heterogeneous strengths, and aggregate event-time scaling, but excludes the information-exponent-two mechanism that the predecessor exploits.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Gaussian Multi-Index Models with Gradient Flow: Time Complexity and Directional Convergence
competitive_landscape.difference: Simsek et al. characterize gradient-flow fixed points under correlation loss, prove nearest-direction convergence for orthogonal teachers with about k log k neurons, and show a correlation threshold where an average-direction minimum appears. The reviewed paper adds finite-step online SGD, unequal power-law coefficients, and MSE deflation, while retaining exact orthogonality and stronger activation restrictions.

competitive_landscape.title: An exactly solvable model for emergence and scaling laws in the multitask sparse parity problem
competitive_landscape.difference: Nam et al. solve independent skill-basis dynamics and fit their sigmoidal emergence and scaling formulas to a two-layer sparse-parity network. The reviewed paper proves approximate task decoupling rather than assuming it, in a Gaussian feature-learning teacher-student model, but supplies much less empirical breadth.

competitive_landscape.title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling
competitive_landscape.difference: Michaud et al. hypothesize discrete quanta learned in frequency order and connect power-law use frequencies to loss scaling, including toy and language-model evidence. The reviewed paper gives a rigorous event-order mechanism and exponent in a narrow shallow Gaussian model, but does not validate it on language models or derive a realistic skill-frequency distribution.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws in Linear Regression: Compute, Parameters, and Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin et al. derive parameter and sample exponents for sketched linear regression with a power-law data spectrum and implicit SGD regularization. The reviewed paper recovers analogous tail exponents from nonlinear feature-search events and a power-law teacher, at the cost of far more restrictive geometry and learning-rate conditions.

competitive_landscape.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon et al. analyze training-time, dataset, width, and compute behavior in a solvable random-feature model, including reused-data train-test gaps. The reviewed paper instead learns the features themselves and proves direction-level emergence, but treats fresh samples and population loss rather than finite-dataset generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning quadratic neural networks in high dimensions: SGD dynamics and scaling laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct subsequent companion at information exponent two
competitive_landscape.difference: Ben Arous et al. analyze essentially the extensive orthogonal, power-law-coefficient teacher setting for quadratic activation using a matrix Riccati equation and monotonicity, covering the information-exponent-two case excluded here. The reviewed paper handles even information exponent above two through sharp scalar search events and greedy deflation rather than joint matrix dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws and Spectra of Shallow Neural Networks in the Feature Learning Regime
competitive_landscape.difference: Defilippis et al. derive sample-complexity and weight-decay phase diagrams for quadratic and diagonal networks and connect excess-risk regimes to learned weight spectra. The reviewed paper focuses on online optimization time, event emergence, and model width under an explicit teacher rather than finite-sample regularized excess risk and spectral phases.

competitive_landscape.title: How Width and Data Shape Generalization Scaling Laws in Quadratic Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Girardin et al. study l2-regularized empirical-risk minimization in a finite-sample quadratic feature-learning model and derive generalization regimes around interpolation. This addresses the fixed-data generalization axis absent from the reviewed online-SGD population theory, while specializing to quadratic networks and a different optimization target.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Quadratic Forms: A Unified Minimal Model for Sudden Learning and Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziyin et al. derive a symmetry-constrained quadratic normal form for several exchangeable architectures, close its dynamics on a second-moment order parameter, and recover both sequential mode ignition and training-time power laws under structured data. The reviewed paper proves online-SGD direction recovery for a specific nonlinear shallow teacher rather than an architecture-level local surrogate, but its scope across architectures and optimizers is much narrower.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Nakamuta and Teramae exactly solve how training changes local power-law representation-spectrum exponents in a wide two-layer linear teacher-student model with power-law input and teacher structure, then test nonlinear analogues. The reviewed paper derives a loss exponent from rank-ordered feature-emergence times under isotropic inputs, not the evolving internal spectrum under anisotropic data.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first polynomial single-phase online-SGD guarantee for extensive-width orthogonal additive teachers with potentially diverging second-layer condition number, together with sharp per-direction recovery times and feature-learning scaling laws in steps, samples, width, and compute.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Same-class additive-feature learnability, multi-index directional convergence, independent-skill emergence models, and linear or random-feature scaling laws all predate the work. Its proposed new combination is simultaneous MSE training under a 2-homogeneous parameterization, approximate automatic deflation at extensive width, preservation of random event-order gaps under online SGD, and integration of those events into a loss exponent.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The intended event-order and one-phase deflation analysis is genuinely distinctive for information exponent above two, but the printed initialization-gap proof, selected-set strength bound, event-time summaries, and Appendix E derivation contain material gaps. The broader scaling-law relevance also remains narrow: this is a realizable isotropic Gaussian model with exact orthogonality, tiny initialization, a special positive parameterization, and highly conservative rates. The asymptotic beta exponents remain plausible heuristics consistent with the intended mechanism, not independently verified consequences of the exact v2 proof.

reviewer_notes: The complete 97-page arXiv v2 extraction was checked twice, including all three figures, the population and sample-gradient formulas, initialization-gap lemma, gradient-flow induction, online-SGD stochastic induction, proof of Theorem 2.1, and Appendix E scaling derivation. Exact PDF and text hashes were reproduced, and a fresh versionless export was byte-identical to v2; v1 is a distinct 100-page artifact. The PDF has no tables, embedded attachments, repository URL, implementation claim, code, or data. The official NeurIPS 2025 version of record (DOI 10.52202/085713-1280) is a distinct 83-page artifact with the same main claims and defects, not the pinned source. Twelve primary arXiv or official-proceedings records were checked at their current versions through 2026-08-24.
